papers.title: Formalizing and Benchmarking Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses
DataSentinel: A Game-Theoretic Detection of Prompt Injection Attacks

meta.policy: code and prompts are linked, not copied; the toolkit was read as text and not executed
meta.mapping: attack to technique and defence to control is an analyst mapping (scripts/open_prompt_injection_check.py)

attacks.name: naive
attacks.description: Appends the injected instruction and data to the target data.

attacks.name: escape
attacks.description: Adds escape characters (such as a newline) so the injected instruction reads as a new segment.

attacks.name: ignore
attacks.description: Adds a context-ignoring sentence that tells the model to disregard previous instructions.

attacks.name: fake_comp
attacks.description: Adds a fake response so the model treats the target task as already completed.

attacks.name: combine
attacks.description: Combines escape characters, a fake completion and a context-ignoring sentence; the strongest strategy in the paper.

defences.name: instructional
defences.description: Warns the model in the instruction that the data may try to change it.

defences.name: sandwich
defences.description: Repeats the task after the data.

defences.name: random_seq
defences.description: Encloses the data between random strings.

defences.name: xml
defences.description: Encloses the data in XML tags.

defences.name: response-based
defences.description: Drops answers that do not fit the target task's label set.

defences.name: ppl
defences.description: Flags data whose perplexity under a surrogate model passes a threshold.

defences.name: retokenization
defences.description: Retokenizes the data with BPE dropout to break crafted sequences.

defences.name: llm-based
defences.description: Asks a model whether the data contains instructions.

defences.name: known-answer
defences.description: Asks the model to repeat a known secret while ignoring the data; a different answer flags injection.

defences.name: paraphrasing
defences.description: Has the model paraphrase the data before the task runs.

detectors.name: DataSentinel
detectors.description: Fine-tuned known-answer detector trained against adaptive attacks (game-theoretic).

detectors.name: PromptLocate
detectors.description: Finds the injected segment inside contaminated data and recovers the clean data.

metrics.PNA: Performance under no attack: how well the model does the task (target or injected) on clean data.
metrics.ASV: Attack success value: how well the model does the injected task when the attack is applied.
metrics.MR: Matching rate: how often answers under attack match the answers to the injected task alone.

lab_mapping.result: ASV and MR under attack, PNA without attack, per attack strategy and defence
lab_mapping.context: model and its config, target task, injected task, number of samples, defence specification
lab_mapping.caveat: A low ASV against a fixed strategy is not robustness: adaptive attacks are outside this matrix.

limits: The applications are single-turn text tasks (sentiment, spam, grammar, summarisation and others). There are no tools, agents, retrieval or memory, so results do not carry over to agent systems.
Attack strategies are fixed templates. They measure baseline exposure, not robustness against an adaptive attacker.

Every defence in the toolkit is in-band: it changes the prompt, the data or the answer, or asks a model to judge. None limits what a hijacked model can do; out-of-band controls (CTRL-POLICY-OUTSIDE-MODEL, CTRL-PRIVILEGE-SEPARATED-LLM, CTRL-DATAFLOW-TAINT) are outside its scope.
before_running: API keys are read from JSON files under configs/model_configs: keep real keys out of the clone and out of version control.

DataSentinel and PromptLocate checkpoints are downloaded from Google Drive links with no published hash or signature: treat them as unverified model artifacts (CTRL-ARTIFACT-PINNING, CTRL-SIGNATURE-VERIFICATION).
One model loader passes trust_remote_code=True to Hugging Face, which runs code shipped with that model: pin the revision or skip that model.
The conda environment pins Python 3.9 and 2024-era libraries: run it in an isolated environment, not next to production tooling.
